translations.text: March 21. The Life of Our Venerable Father Isaac of the Monastery of Dalmatus.
After the veneration of the most holy and revered cross of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ,
when idol worship had already been rejected, all things under heaven
were enlightened by the apostles’ preaching. For the honorable Emperor Constantine also,
at a later time, through the divine Spirit, received dominion over the empire of the whole inhabited world,
and was found worthy of holy illumination and came to know that our Lord Jesus Christ is the true God.
He was the first emperor to reign in the city of Rome and reject the idols.
But the many-headed serpent of many forms, the devil, invented another form of idol worship,
the Arian blasphemy. For in the days of the aforementioned Christian Emperor Constantine,
there was a certain priest of the holy Church of God in Alexandria, a destroyer in appearance,
and the first inventor of every blasphemy of the devil, the enemy of our souls.
He, by the holy bishop and martyr Peter, through a revelation from God,
was excluded from priestly ministry.
The circumstances of his exclusion were these. When Saint Peter had been seized by soldiers
whom Emperor Diocletian had sent to kill him, and had been thrown
into prison, as he was praying at midnight according to his custom, he saw a handsome young man standing before him,
clothed in a linen tunic torn from top to bottom,
holding it with both hands by the two edges of the garment,
and covering his nakedness so that Peter would not see his bare chest.
Suddenly Saint Peter opened his mouth and said, “Lord, who has torn your tunic?”
He replied, “Arius has torn it in two for me. But take care not to forgive him or receive him into communion,
and do not lift his excommunication. For Arius, both in the present age and in the age to come,
shall be excluded from the glory of God. Now summon Achillas and Alexander, both priests,
because, when you have completed your martyrdom, these two will succeed to the bishop’s throne in turn.
Command them that they too must not receive him into communion.” And when the Lord had said this,
he disappeared from his sight. Having done all this, the venerable Bishop Peter
ended his life in a good confession of faith. When Arius realized that he remained excommunicated, he began
to speak with blasphemous lips everywhere in Alexandria against the consubstantial and holy Trinity,
and openly to distort the divine Scriptures, saying that the Son and Word of God,
begotten of him without beginning before the ages, was foreign to the Father's essence.
And the defiled and impure man dared to rank among created things the one through whom all things came into being,
those in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. When these things eventually reached the ears
of the aforementioned honorable Emperor Constantine, he did not overlook them, but wrote and sent letters, urging him,
sometimes with instruction and sometimes with censure, to desist henceforth from such God-defying blasphemy.
And when he learned that Arius persisted in the same way, without correcting that evil, he immediately ordered Arius to leave Alexandria
and come quickly to Constantinople, to answer for how he had dared to blaspheme God.
Then the emperor gathered the holy bishops from everywhere in the city of Nicaea, 318 in number.
He told them about the invention of that senseless, God-defying heresy and urged them to pray to the Lord
Christ, that he would join the struggle for the true and right faith. These most praiseworthy fathers,
having the Holy Spirit as their fellow worker and being inspired by him,
rejected the invention of the heresy resembling that of the Jews, and those more recent than it.
They overcame it through their prayers. For when he had come from the city of Alexandria
and entered the assembly of the holy ones, with senseless arrogance lending him support,
he professed his foul blasphemy. But the godly fathers exposed the deception
and handed down the true and indivisible faith in the shared essence of the Trinity
to all the faithful living under the sun, telling Emperor Constantine
to believe likewise, as one who shared the throne in establishing the right faith.
He accepted it and believed that the faithful tradition was from God; and to honor and accept it,
and, by imperial decree, everywhere throughout the whole earth to uphold this faith in the shared essence
of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, he commanded. But leaving much aside, let us come to the main subject. For of all the visible ages
and God, who provides for invisible things, who was blasphemed by Arius before men and counted among created things.
He was driven by a movement of his bowels, and into a place for excrement [?] his unclean bowels.
Having expelled all his bowels, that unclean man [?], again shining like a lamp.
He lived until the departure of the venerable fathers and met an end worthy of his life.
For it was fitting that the man who had made himself stink with blasphemies against Christ should end his life in a stinking place.
While these miracles were being performed so gloriously by the Lord Jesus Christ,
after a year had passed, the enemy of the world, Belial [?], set up his own instrument, Emperor Valens, like a second Arius, against the true faith.
He was exceedingly lawless and like another Ahab.
He raged against the holy churches of God, renewing all the blasphemy of Arius.
And he ordered all the holy churches of God belonging to the orthodox to be closed,
and the customary services not to be held in them. Some of them he turned into sheds,
and others he even attempted to demolish. Such inconsolable sorrow continued for many
years. At that same time there was a certain man in the desert in the East,
living an angelic life on earth, named Isaac. As was his custom,
he heard God's voice from heaven, commanding him to come down from the desert and go to the city of Constantine.
He did not disobey, but came down from the desert and arrived in the city that had been named. He found a soul-destroying flood of heresy opposed to God.
And, as with the compassionate prophet Jeremiah, a fire flared up within him.
And he went about everywhere. By the permission of God, who always disciplines us for our benefit,
a great war arose against the pagans. They gathered their forces and crossed the river called the Danube,
and laid waste to Thrace. The inhabitants of the city suffered great distress and sorrow.
Then Emperor Valens also gathered his soldiers and prepared to march out against the enemy.
And as he was going out into the field to inspect his soldiers, our holy father, inflamed by the Holy Spirit,
like another Daniel defending Susanna—our holy father Isaac—
approached the impious man and said, “Emperor, open the churches of the orthodox, and the Lord will make your path straight
before you.” But he, seeing the old man in such a poor state and dressed in rags,
He ignored him and did not answer him a single word, for at that time there was not even a trace of a monk there.
Then again, the next morning, as he was going out, he stood before him and said, “Emperor,
open the churches of the orthodox, and you will overcome your enemies and return in peace.”
The emperor, grasping the force of the words the saint had spoken, “You will return in peace,”
consulted with his advisers about opening the churches. But the chamberlain and the others,
who belonged to the evil faith of Arius, led the emperor further astray.
They mocked him, laughed at his words, and struck him with whips.
The emperor listened to them, ignored him, and went away. But the servant of God prayed to God unceasingly
that he would quickly bring help to the true faith. After two days, the emperor drew up his troops
and was setting out for war. But the blessed man intercepted him on the road and approached him.
Taking hold of his horse’s bridle, he tried to stop him, saying, “Open the churches of the orthodox.”
But he, as was his custom, remained unyielding
and those near the emperor beat the man to make him withdraw.
They could not pull him away. An uproar arose over this, and many people came running together.
They all beat him in different ways, some with rods, some with whips,
and others with staffs. And only with difficulty, when God had allowed [?],
were they able to pull his hands away from the bridle of the emperor’s horse.
Then the emperor Valens flew into a rage. Looking this way and that, he saw a certain place,
like a dried-up pit, full of stinking mud, with dense woodland in it,
and very fierce thorns and brambles. If any animal fell into that place, it would never come out alive.
The emperor examined that place and, realizing that it was a deathtrap, ordered him to be thrown into it.
Then he went on his way. But when the valiant confessor of Christ, Isaac, had been thrown
into that deadly abyss, he remained unharmed, suffering no injury at all.
For immediately, by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, two angels came and pulled him out of that mud.
They brought him out, set him on the road, and said to him, “Peace be with you. Be strong and courageous.” And having said this,
The two went away from him. Coming to himself, he knelt down and thanked God,
who cares for his servants in many ways. Then, rising from prayer,
he ran by another road and reached the emperor ahead of him. Again taking hold of the emperor’s horse by its bridle,
he said boldly to the emperor, “You, emperor, wanted to kill me by throwing me into the mire.
But the Lord Jesus Christ, whom you blaspheme, kept me alive and brought me out of your trap
to expose your rebellious mind. Even now I urge you: listen to me
and open the churches of the orthodox believers and restore them to them. You will prevail in the war to which you are going
and return in peace, and there will be praise upon praise.” When the emperor saw the blessed man, the radiance of his face,
and his boldness of speech, he was so beside himself that he could not answer him a word.
Then, after a little while, the emperor said to the blessed man, “But if I do not open or restore the churches of the orthodox believers,
what will happen because of that?” Then Christ’s servant, angered through the Holy Spirit,
following the prophet Elijah’s example against Ahab, king of Israel, now likewise
prophesied to Emperor Valens, saying, “It would have been well for you, emperor, to listen to me,
to open and restore the churches of the orthodox believers, and to go and return in peace.
But since you have not listened to me or yielded, if you go to war and return alive, then know that the Lord has not spoken through me now.
For you will go to war and join battle, and you will be unable to stand against your enemies.
You will flee from them, and they will pursue you, and you will run into a house.
There you will be burned alive in the fire. Then, in the hour of your distress, you will know
that there is a God in heaven whom you blaspheme.” When Emperor Valens heard this,
he summoned two noblemen, one named Saturninus and the other Victor.
He handed the holy man over to them, saying, “Shut him in prison with every kind of hardship,
and put chains around his neck until I return and put him to death, after his empty prophecy.”
Then blessed Isaac smiled a little and said to the emperor, “I have already told you:
if you return alive, then the Lord has not spoken through me.” The emperor went on his way.
And the two distinguished men mentioned earlier took blessed Isaac with them.
They led him away and imprisoned him, as the emperor had commanded them. After the holy man entered the prison,
he never ceased, night and day, praying to God with tears to look upon his flock and quickly send it help.
When the emperor reached a city near the Danube, he reviewed his troops and consulted with them.
He appointed a day on which to engage the enemy. But when he engaged them, he could not withstand them.
Instead, he turned his back and fled from them. They pursued him, and as he fled he reached a village.
Finding an open barn, he rushed into it with the chamberlain,
who had been corrupting his soul. When the pursuing pagans saw that he had rushed into the barn as he fled,
they took fire and set the barn alight, burning him inside it.
And there, in torment, he gave up his soul, according to the prophecy of Isaac, the servant of God.
The surviving soldiers came to the city of Sirmium and sent messengers to Emperor Gratian, reporting
everything that had happened. He immediately came to the aforementioned city of Sirmium and, by God's appointment,
appointed an emperor for them named Theodosius, a faithful, Christ-loving man of orthodox belief.
Though still unbaptized, he was courageous and brave. By the joint decision of the two emperors,
they prepared for war against the pagans who had burned Emperor Valens. And with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ,
they killed some of them and drove the others away. Most of them drowned in the Danube as they fled.
Thus the emperors Gratian and Theodosius won the victory. After this victory,
Emperor Gratian went to Rome, and Theodosius to Constantinople.
When he reached the city of Thessalonica, he was struck by disease and fell ill. He summoned the bishop of Thessalonica, named Acholius,
and asked what faith he held. He replied, “The Arian blasphemy has not reached the western regions,
nor has the impious opposition to God that arose through it been able to lead them astray.
Instead, we hold the faith handed down from the beginning by the apostles.” Then Emperor Theodosius received this with reverence,
asking for holy baptism. And he was baptized by Acholius, the bishop of Thessalonica who was there,
in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Having recovered,
after many days he came to Constantinople. At that time Bishop Gregory of Nazianzus
was holding assemblies in a small church within the city, gathering the people and strengthening them through his teaching.
On the true faith. This church was later built at the emperor’s command and was called Anastasia.
The two noblemen who had thrown blessed Isaac into prison, Saturninus and Victor,
entered the prison and said to blessed Isaac, “Pray to God, father,
for the emperor has defeated his enemies, and now he is coming.” Smiling a little, he said to them,
“I know, my child, that the faithful emperor Theodosius is coming. For the evildoer Valens
has received a judgment like yours, together with the chamberlain. The stench of their burning is still in my nostrils.”
Then the two men marveled, bowed down, and immediately went out.
They met the emperor and told him everything concerning Saint Isaac
and his prophecy, which he had spoken to the face of the wretched Valens,
and how it had come true for him. When the emperor heard this, he marveled at the man and immediately ordered
that he be brought with every honor into the emperor’s palace. The two distinguished men hurried to the prison
and fell at the feet of the holy man, begging him to pray to God for them, for they had realized that he was a prophet,
since all his prophecies had come true. They brought him out of prison and took him to the emperor.
The emperor came out to meet him, bowed down to him, and asked for his prayers.
The saint prayed and kissed him, and told him everything concerning the impious Valens.
When he heard this, the emperor grieved over the affliction of the holy churches and immediately decreed a punishment.
He wrote letters and sent them to the designated places, commanding as follows: “Emperor Theodosius,
victor and sovereign ruler, to all Arian [?]: Let it be known to you
that from this day onward, if any of you is found gathering within the city in a church of the orthodox,
he shall receive the death penalty. And as for the holy churches that you have seized by force, leave them too and remain outside the city.”
He also sent word to their leader, who was at that time the leader of the Arians,
named Demophilus, saying: “Believe in the decrees of the Council of Nicaea and be reconciled with the orthodox.”
But when Demophilus rejected the emperor’s command, and unity and reconciliation,
the emperor delivered this pronouncement to him: “You flee from peace and unity;
therefore I command you to flee from the holy churches.” When Demophilus heard this,
Calling all the Arians together in the church, he said to them: Brothers,
the emperor is humane and asks for a church for his own faith, having informed us gently.
“The churches,” he said, “which you seized through war and turmoil, you shall hand back peacefully.”
Know, then, that from this day onward we have been ordered to assemble outside the city.
Having said this, he went outside the city with his people and thereafter held assemblies there.
Thus the Arians had held the churches of the orthodox for as long as forty years.
But by Theodosius, the Christian emperor,
they were driven out not only from the churches but also from the city, and the orthodox took possession of the churches.
Without delay, the emperor convened a council of bishops to confirm the orthodox faith,
the Nicene faith, and to appoint a bishop in Constantinople,
and to establish order for the holy churches and all the people. Emperor Theodosius also commanded
the leaders of the heretics to come to the council. The adherents of the consubstantial faith gathered:
Timothy from Alexandria, Cyril from Jerusalem, and Meletius from Antioch.
Gregory of Nazianzus was also there, and Acholius from Thessalonica, and many others with them.
There were 150 in all. From the party of Arius and Macedonius
came Eleusius, Marcian of Lampsacus, and Euthius [?] of Ephesus,
and Maris of Chalcedon and others; there were thirty-six in all. Most of them were from the cities of the Hellespont
and of Asia. They gathered in the month of May. The bishops and the emperor
and our holy father Isaac the Confessor made every effort, wishing to unite them
with the orthodox and consubstantial faith. But they paid little heed to this,
and, regarding the exhortations as of no account, said:
“We prefer the Arian faith to accepting consubstantiality.” And when they had said this,
they were expelled from the church council and even from the city itself,
having rejected the orthodox faith. After jointly confirming the holy orthodox Nicene faith,
they also laid down a rule of faith. But the emperor, concerning the appointment of a bishop of Constantinople,
He told the bishops to appoint someone. And they nominated a certain Nectarius, a distinguished and devout man,
gentle in manner, from a noble family, who then held the office of prefect.
He was brought forward by the people for the bishopric and was ordained by the holy fathers, with 108 present there,
along with the Christ-loving Emperor Theodosius and our venerable father Isaac.
Then they established a rule that the bishop of Constantinople
should have the same precedence and the same honor as the bishop of Rome,
because it had been called New Rome. When all these things had thus taken place, the council of bishops soon came
to an end, to the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. Then the blessed Isaac rejoiced in the restoration of order in the Church
and of the true faith, and he glorified God for all the wonders he had performed. He was considering going immediately into the wilderness,
from which he had come here through a revelation from God, for the work that he had now completed.
When the frequently mentioned distinguished men Saturninus and Victor learned this, they approached the holy man
and begged him not to leave them. But he, like a spiritual father, sought to restrain them, saying,
“Since the Lord has helped us complete the work for which he sent us, it is fitting for me to return
and devote myself to my own work of self-discipline.” But those two faithful men begged him with tears
to grant their request. When the blessed man understood the spiritual love they had for him,
he said to them, “My desire is indeed to return to the place from which I came.
But since you lovingly wish to provide comfort for my lowly self as a servant of Christ,
listen to what I tell you as a father. Whichever
of you is first to make me a little dwelling where I can stay, there I will live until the departure of my soul.”
Those two men listened to his holy words, and both competed
to see which of them would be first to build him a cell. Saturninus had an estate outside the city,
not far from the city, and Victor likewise had one by the seashore.
Both began to build in the name of the blessed Isaac. But Saturninus, exercising great wisdom,
rightly considered that this man was accustomed to a life of silence
and did not now need splendid dwellings, so he built him a two-story cell.
And after finishing it in every detail, he came to the blessed man and said to him, “Look, I have built the cell just as you commanded.
Go in and live in it.” And our holy father went into the cell, and when he saw that it was quiet,
he was pleased with it and settled there with great eagerness. Victor, meanwhile, had set aside a large area
for many large dwellings. But when he learned that Saturninus had acted before him,
he was deeply saddened, and he went into the cell to the venerable man.
He bowed before him, begging him to accept also the place built in his name.
But the venerable man, like a father who loves his children, reasoned with him, saying, “No, my child,
do not trouble yourself so much. It is the Lord’s commandment that says: Let your yes be yes,
and your no, no; whatever goes beyond this comes from the evil one. So the place where the Lord has granted me to settle
is where I must remain in silence until the end of my life.”
And after praying for them, he sent them away in peace. And the blessed Isaac lived an angelic life.
The two illustrious men mentioned so often would not go to the palace to see the emperor
without first going to the venerable man early at dawn and bowing before him.
And after receiving his blessing, they would depart rejoicing. By telling many others
about the venerable man, they stirred them to spiritual zeal.
And people came to him from everywhere every day, being built up and strengthened
in faith in the Lord by his holy words. Many also begged him to come to their homes
to pray to God for them. Seeing their faith and showing that he did not disdain them, he would go.
And if he happened to be delayed at someone’s home, he would leave at night.
And when the city gates were shut, he would stand and offer a prayer to God.
He would make the sign of the cross over the gates, and they would open by themselves. And so he would return to his cell.
The faithful emperor Theodosius also came to him and begged him to remember him in his holy prayers.
And the Lord, who said, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am among them,”
was pleased, for the glory of his holy name, to increase his servant’s flock of people.
For just as a loud trumpet, when sounded, rouses many to muster for battle,
Thus the heavenly life of our venerable father Isaac was proclaimed everywhere and to everyone.
He brought many to this angelic way of life, for there had not yet been a single monk there.
Then Saturninus, seeing the brotherhood increasing by God’s grace and having great love for the servant of God,
gave him that entire estate, to be under his authority for a monastery.
The blessed man was like a lamp shining in a dark place.
Whenever he happened to go into the cities with those who had invited him into their homes for a blessing,
and one of the poor asked him to give him something,
if he happened to have nothing to give him,
he would take off his cloak and give it to the poor man. He did this throughout all the years of his life,
serving the Lord, persevering in prayer, offering hospitality to strangers, and championing care for the poor.
He commemorated the saints and was bold in doing good, peaceable, innocent, free from anger, and devoted to teaching.
With gentleness he taught those who came to him the true faith, instructing them and bearing witness concerning all things,
that they should confess and glorify the undivided and consubstantial Trinity,
the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since upon this reverent confession human salvation
rests. Teaching many other things as well, he never ceased or fell silent in doing good.
Having grown old to a good old age, he reached the end of his life. He gathered together his entire spiritual flock in Christ,
and instructed them at length to remain upon the firm and unshakable rock of faith in the Lord.
He entrusted [?] to the most merciful God. There was mourning among the brothers on his account.
The Christian emperor Theodosius also heard that he had fallen asleep.
He grieved deeply and sent a [?], so that they might place the venerable man’s honored body in it
and bring it to the great church, which was then called Irene, and from there carry it onward for burial.
When this had been done, they held an all-night vigil in the aforementioned church.
Then, the next morning, the whole city, together with the archbishop and all the clergy,
carried him with praises and spiritual songs, accompanying him all the way to his burial.
Now Aurelian, one of the emperor’s distinguished men, opposite the monastery of Father Isaac, […]
To the north he built a church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. At the time when the thrice-blessed
Isaac was being carried out, he stationed a large crowd of men as helpers on the road in front of the monastery,
so that they might take up and carry the relics of our holy father Isaac
to the aforementioned church for a blessing, and lay him there, as indeed happened.
Thus he chose to be laid in the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, to the right of the holy altar,
inside the sanctuary. His disciples, grieving, returned to the monastery,
which was not far from the aforementioned church. Our holy father and confessor Isaac died
on March 21, during the reign of the Christ-loving Emperor Theodosius,
to the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
